query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy designed with a tailored mix of magnetic and non‐magnetic elements can exhibit an enhanced magnetocaloric effect due to a broadened and tunable magnetic phase transition.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HEA) in a simple solid solution phase (e.g., FCC or BCC) with a random distribution of multiple elements.
generation.intervention: Adjust the compositional balance by incorporating elements with strong magnetic moments alongside other metals to tune the magnetic interactions and shift the Curie temperature closer to the working temperature range.
generation.conditions: The alloy is evaluated under controlled temperature sweeps near its magnetic transition temperature and subjected to an external magnetic field during measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Random solid solution structure derived from high configurational entropy, which enables distributed and tunable magnetic exchange interactions.
generation.mechanism: The presence of multiple elements in near-equiatomic ratios leads to local variations in the magnetic exchange interactions. This broadens the magnetic phase transition and increases the entropy change upon application or removal of a magnetic field, thereby improving the magnetocaloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA will show a larger magnetic entropy change and adiabatic temperature change near its Curie point compared to conventional binary or low-entropy alloys.
generation.baseline: Conventional magnetocaloric materials (e.g., Gd-based alloys or Ni-rich alloys) that typically have sharper magnetic transitions and more limited tunability.
generation.boundary: The advantage is expected to diminish if excessive non-magnetic element addition or phase segregation occurs, which could disrupt the uniform magnetic interaction network necessary for an effective magnetocaloric response.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of enhancement in the magnetocaloric effect and the optimal balance of magnetic versus non-magnetic elements in the HEA cannot be predicted without targeted experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one set consisting of a baseline HEA composition and the other with the adjusted magnetic element composition. Subject both sets to identical temperature sweeps and magnetic field cycles. Compare the magnetocaloric properties (magnetic entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) around the Curie temperature.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔSm) as a function of temperature and applied magnetic field
Adiabatic temperature change (ΔTad) near the magnetic transition
Structural analyses (XRD, TEM) to confirm single-phase solid solution
Magnetic characterization (VSM or SQUID) to assess the Curie temperature and magnetic ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified HEA does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ΔSm or ΔTad compared to the baseline HEA under identical testing conditions, or if severe phase segregation is observed that negates the predicted broadening of the magnetic phase transition, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
